claim: Colorectal cancer (CRC) organoids can be derived from almost all CRC patients.
source: Colorectal cancer (CRC) organoids can be derived from almost all CRC patients and therefore capture the genetic diversity of this disease.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract without specific experimental data provided in this sentence, but is supported by the citation to van de Wetering et al., 2015 elsewhere in the manuscript.

claim: CRC organoids capture the genetic diversity of colorectal cancer disease.
source: Colorectal cancer (CRC) organoids can be derived from almost all CRC patients and therefore capture the genetic diversity of this disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by the establishment of a genetically diverse biobank as described in the manuscript and referenced to van de Wetering et al., 2015.

claim: Presence of mutant RAS correlated strongly with resistance to targeted therapies in CRC organoids.
source: Presence of mutant RAS correlated strongly with resistance to these targeted therapies.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures including dose-response curves and viability assays comparing RAS WT and RAS mutant organoids.

claim: Resistance to targeted therapies was observed in both tumorigenic and normal organoids with mutant RAS.
source: This was observed in tumorigenic as well as in normal organoids.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing normal and tumor organoids with and without KRAS mutations shown in Figures 5 and related supplementary figures.

claim: Dual inhibition of the EGFR-MEK-ERK pathway in RAS mutant organoids induced a transient cell-cycle arrest rather than cell death.
source: Moreover, dual inhibition of the EGFR-MEK-ERK pathway in RAS mutant organoids induced a transient cell-cycle arrest rather than cell death.
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging data, flow cytometry cell cycle analysis, and EdU incorporation experiments shown in Figures 1, 3, 7, and 8.

claim: In vivo drug response of xenotransplanted RAS mutant organoids confirmed growth arrest upon pan-HER/MEK combination therapy.
source: In vivo drug response of xenotransplanted RAS mutant organoids confirmed this growth arrest upon pan-HER/MEK combination therapy.
evidence: This is supported by xenograft experiments shown in Figure 2 where tumor growth stabilization was observed with high-dose combination therapy.

claim: RAS mutations occur in about 15% of all human tumors.
source: RAS mutations occur in about 15% of all human tumors (Bos, 1989) and so far all attempts to selectively interfere in mutant RAS signaling have failed in the clinic (Stephen et al., 2014; Cox et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bos, 1989.

claim: All attempts to selectively interfere in mutant RAS signaling have failed in the clinic.
source: RAS mutations occur in about 15% of all human tumors (Bos, 1989) and so far all attempts to selectively interfere in mutant RAS signaling have failed in the clinic (Stephen et al., 2014; Cox et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Stephen et al., 2014 and Cox et al., 2014.

claim: Cell lines have very limited genetic diversity as model systems.
source: Progress has long been impeded by the fact that the currently used model systems to pre-test drugs are insufficient: cell lines, on the one hand, have very limited genetic diversity, while mouse models on the other hand, may not represent human tumors (Sachs and Clevers, 2014; Gould et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sachs and Clevers, 2014 and Gould et al., 2015.

claim: Mouse models may not represent human tumors.
source: Progress has long been impeded by the fact that the currently used model systems to pre-test drugs are insufficient: cell lines, on the one hand, have very limited genetic diversity, while mouse models on the other hand, may not represent human tumors (Sachs and Clevers, 2014; Gould et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sachs and Clevers, 2014 and Gould et al., 2015.

claim: Stem-cell based organoid technology can establish long-term cultures of both normal and tumor tissues from various organs.
source: Recently, stem-cell based organoid technology was introduced to establish long-term cultures of both normal and tumor tissues from various organs (Sato et al., 2009, 2011; Bartfeld et al., 2015; Boj et al., 2015; Huch et al., 2015; Karthaus et al., 2014; Gao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published work on organoid technology.

claim: Organoid technology can capture the genetic diversity of both normal and tumor tissues.
source: The advantage of this technology is that it can capture the genetic diversity of both normal and tumor tissues.
evidence: This is supported by the establishment and characterization of diverse organoid biobanks as described in the manuscript and referenced literature.

claim: A genetically diverse Biobank of patient-derived CRC organoids was established.
source: Indeed, for colorectal cancer (CRC) a genetically diverse Biobank of patient-derived CRC organoids was established and used to integrate genomic data and monotherapy drug responses at the level of individual patient-derived organoid lines (van de Wetering et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to van de Wetering et al., 2015.

claim: P8T organoid contains wild-type KRAS.
source: P8T contains wild-type (WT) KRAS, while P26T contains an oncogenic mutant version of KRAS (G12V).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section describing the organoid lines used.

claim: P26T organoid contains oncogenic mutant KRAS (G12V).
source: P8T contains wild-type (WT) KRAS, while P26T contains an oncogenic mutant version of KRAS (G12V).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section describing the organoid lines used.

claim: P8T is sensitive to afatinib treatment.
source: We observed the expected sensitivity of P8T towards afatinib (irreversible EGFR/HER2 inhibitor) and insensitivity of KRAS mutant P26T (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response curve data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: KRAS mutant P26T is insensitive to afatinib treatment.
source: We observed the expected sensitivity of P8T towards afatinib (irreversible EGFR/HER2 inhibitor) and insensitivity of KRAS mutant P26T (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response curve data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Selumetinib as a monotherapy showed little efficacy in both P8T and P26T.
source: Selumetinib (MEKi) as a monotherapy showed little efficacy in both P8T and P26T, but combination therapy confirmed previous findings that MEKi sensitizes RAS mutant tumor cells to EGFR/HER2 inhibition (Figure 1A) (Sun et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data in Figure 1A.

claim: MEK inhibitor sensitizes RAS mutant tumor cells to EGFR/HER2 inhibition.
source: Selumetinib (MEKi) as a monotherapy showed little efficacy in both P8T and P26T, but combination therapy confirmed previous findings that MEKi sensitizes RAS mutant tumor cells to EGFR/HER2 inhibition (Figure 1A) (Sun et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data in Figure 1A and citation to Sun et al., 2014.

claim: KRAS mutant P26T organoids were less sensitive to afatinib/selumetinib combination therapy than KRAS WT P8T organoids.
source: However, the KRAS mutant P26T organoids were less sensitive to the combination therapy than the KRAS WT P8T organoids.
evidence: This is supported by dose-response curves shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In P26T (mutant KRAS), afatinib and selumetinib combination treatment resulted in cell cycle arrest with very limited cell death induction.
source: In P26T (mutant KRAS) we only observed cell cycle arrest with very limited cell death induction.
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1B and Video 1.

claim: Afatinib and selumetinib combination treatment induced very rapid cell death in P8T (WT KRAS).
source: This was in stark contrast with the very rapid induction of cell death in P8T (WT KRAS) (Figure 1B, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1B and Video 1.

claim: Only P26T CRC organoids showed reliable engraftment in xenotransplantation experiments.
source: In line with a previous report where only engineered tumor progression organoids with increasing number of cancer mutations (APC, KRAS, P53 and/or SMAD4) showed efficient engraftment (Drost et al., 2015), we only obtained reliable engraftment using P26T CRC organoids.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Drost et al., 2015 and the experimental results described.

claim: Initial drug concentration schedules of afatinib and selumetinib showed no significant effect on P26T tumor growth in vivo.
source: We initially started using concentration schedules of afatinib and selumetinib that had previously been reported (Sun et al., 2014), but we observed no significant effect of the drug combination on tumor growth over time (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Secondary organoids isolated from drug-treated tumors showed identical drug sensitivity to parental P26T organoids.
source: Dose-response curves on these secondary organoids were identical to the parental organoid line P26T, independent of the type of drug treatment that the tumors underwent in the mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: High doses of afatinib and selumetinib induced significant growth stabilization of P26T xenotransplanted tumors in mice.
source: To confirm this hypothesis, we further increased the drug levels to high but tolerable doses. This indeed induced significant growth stabilization (but no regression) of P26T xenotransplanted tumor in mice (Figure 2B), in agreement with loss of proliferative activity as was also detected in vitro (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In vivo xenografted CRC organoids yield similar drug responses as in vitro organoid cultures.
source: The fact that in vivo xenografted CRC organoids yields similar drug responses as in vitro organoid cultures and identical to previous reported drug response of KRAS mutant PDX models of CRC (Sun et al., 2014), validates the testing and evaluation of targeted inhibitors in CRC organoids.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of in vitro and in vivo data and citation to Sun et al., 2014.

claim: P8T and P26T CRCs are microsatellite-stable (MSS).
source: P8T and P26T CRCs are microsatellite-stable (MSS) and belong to the same molecular subtype classification based on RNA expression data (TA, also referred to as canonical CMS2 according to consensus classification) (van de Wetering et al., 2015; Guinney et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to van de Wetering et al., 2015 and Guinney et al., 2015.

claim: P8T and P26T belong to the same molecular subtype classification (TA/CMS2).
source: P8T and P26T CRCs are microsatellite-stable (MSS) and belong to the same molecular subtype classification based on RNA expression data (TA, also referred to as canonical CMS2 according to consensus classification) (van de Wetering et al., 2015; Guinney et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to van de Wetering et al., 2015 and Guinney et al., 2015.

claim: P8T has 230 cancer-specific mutations in the protein coding sequence.
source: For P8T and P26T, 230 and 163 of such cancer specific mutations were detected respectively (van de Wetering et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to van de Wetering et al., 2015.

claim: P26T has 163 cancer-specific mutations in the protein coding sequence.
source: For P8T and P26T, 230 and 163 of such cancer specific mutations were detected respectively (van de Wetering et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to van de Wetering et al., 2015.

claim: P18T-KRASG12D mutant cells were generated using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated homologous recombination.
source: P18T-KRASG12D mutant cells were generated as reported previously for normal colon organoids (Drost et al., 2015) and genotyping of clonally expanded organoids confirmed that the clones contained the KRASG12D mutation (Figure 3A), as well as a Cas9-mediated inactivation of the second allele by introducing an 86 bp deletion.
evidence: This is supported by the schematic in Figure 3A and citation to Drost et al., 2015.

claim: P18T-KRASG12D contains a Cas9-mediated 86 bp deletion in the second KRAS allele.
source: P18T-KRASG12D mutant cells were generated as reported previously for normal colon organoids (Drost et al., 2015) and genotyping of clonally expanded organoids confirmed that the clones contained the KRASG12D mutation (Figure 3A), as well as a Cas9-mediated inactivation of the second allele by introducing an 86 bp deletion.
evidence: This is supported by the sequencing data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: No overall differences in morphology or growth rates were observed in P18T-KRASG12D compared to P18T during normal culture conditions.
source: Upon addition of oncogenic KRAS, no overall differences in morphology or growth rates were observed during normal culture conditions.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the culture experiments.

claim: Introduction of oncogenic KRAS in P18T provided resistance to EGFR/HER2 inhibition.
source: While the original P18T demonstrated high sensitivity to EGFR/HER2 inhibition by monotherapy, a single introduced oncogenic point mutation in KRAS provided resistance to EGFR/HER2 inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by the full matrix screen data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Presence of oncogenic KRAS renders loss of viability and positive Bliss range towards higher drug concentrations indicating resistance.
source: The heat map of Bliss scores for P18T and P18T-KRAS shows that a large range of concentrations for both compounds show positive scores, but that presence of oncogenic KRAS renders the loss of viability and positive Bliss range towards higher drug concentrations indicating resistance (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Bliss score analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: P18T-KRASG12D showed reduced proliferation but unchanged apoptosis rates upon afatinib/selumetinib treatment.
source: More specifically, quantifications of all mitotic and apoptotic events during the filmed drug response revealed both loss of proliferation and apoptosis induction in P18T, while P18T-KRASG12D only showed reduced proliferation but unchanged apoptosis rates (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of mitotic and apoptotic events shown in Figure 3D.

claim: pERK levels in both P18T and P18T-KRASG12D tumor organoids were severely reduced by afatinib/selumetinib treatment.
source: Despite the phenotypic difference in drug response, pERK levels in both tumor organoids were severely reduced (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Suboptimal suppression of ERK activity might permit tumor growth in BRAF mutant cancers.
source: Since suboptimal suppression of ERK activity might permit tumor growth in BRAF mutant cancers (Bollag et al., 2010; Corcoran et al., 2015), we determined the cellular effects of drug response when lowering drug concentrations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bollag et al., 2010 and Corcoran et al., 2015.

claim: Drug response profiles of normal organoids to targeted inhibitors against the EGFR-RAS-ERK pathway revealed a similar trend as in CRC organoid P18T.
source: Strikingly, drug response profiles of normal organoids to targeted inhibitors against the EGFR-RAS-ERK pathway (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2) revealed a similar trend as in CRC organoid P18T (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of drug response data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The effect that oncogenic KRAS imposes on drug response appears independent of cellular status and the presence of additional cancer mutations.
source: Thus, the effect that oncogenic KRAS imposes on drug response appears independent of cellular status and the presence of additional cancer mutations.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of normal and tumor organoids with and without KRAS mutations showing similar drug response patterns.

claim: No overall phenotypic differences in morphology and proliferative activity were observed upon introduction of oncogenic KRAS in normal colon organoids.
source: In analogy with mouse studies (Snippert et al., 2014), we observed no morphological alteration nor induction of senescence upon introduction of oncogenic KRAS (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and citation to Snippert et al., 2014.

claim: P25T contains an oncogenic mutation in NRAS (Q61H).
source: The first was P25T, which, although WT for KRAS, turned out to contain an oncogenic mutation in NRAS (Q61H), thereby fully explaining the resistant behavior.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the characterization of the organoid panel.

claim: P19bT is characterized as microsatellite instable (MSI) with a hyper-mutator phenotype.
source: The second exception was organoid line P19bT that, unlike the other CRC organoids in our panel, is characterized as microsatellite instable (MSI) including the hyper-mutator phenotype (van de Wetering et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to van de Wetering et al., 2015.

claim: P19bT tumor contains a BRAF (V600E) mutation.
source: Most importantly, P19bT tumor contains a BRAF (V600E) mutation, providing resistance towards the targeted drugs (Di Nicolantonio et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by citation to Di Nicolantonio et al., 2008.

claim: Drug screening on human organoids is able to evaluate the functionality of entire oncogenic pathways beyond the scope of the most frequent candidate mutations.
source: Thus, these two cases underscore that drug screening on human organoids is able to evaluate the functionality of entire oncogenic pathways beyond the scope of the most frequent candidate mutations.
evidence: This is inferred from the identification of NRAS and BRAF mutations explaining drug resistance patterns.

claim: In all seven independent CRC patients with a mutant RAS pathway, synergistic activity was observed when combining EGFRi and MEKi or EGFRi and ERKi.
source: In all seven independent CRC patients with a mutant RAS pathway, we observed synergistic activity when combining EGFRi and MEKi (Sun et al., 2014) or EGFRi and ERKi (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by IC50 data shown in Figure 6B and citation to Sun et al., 2014.

claim: RAS WT organoids reveal higher sensitivities to combination therapies that include EGFR inhibition than RAS mutant CRCs.
source: Nevertheless, RAS WT organoids, either of CRC or normal origin, reveal higher sensitivities to combination therapies that include EGFR inhibition than RAS mutant CRCs.
evidence: This is supported by IC50 comparison data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Therapies that do not include EGFR inhibition but target MEK and ERK were similarly effective in all organoid lines regardless of RAS pathway mutational status or cellular state.
source: In contrast, therapies that do not include EGFR inhibition, but target MEK (selumetinib) and ERK (SCH772984), were similarly effective in all organoid lines, regardless of the mutational status of the RAS pathway or cellular state (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by IC50 data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Combining EGFRi with either MEK or ERKi results in a more consistent inhibitory effect over a set of CRCs than anti-EGFR monotherapy.
source: Combining EGFRi with either MEK or ERKi results in a more consistent inhibitory effect over this set of CRCs (Figure 6B, lower panels), thereby not only improving individual responses but also augmenting success rates on a population scale.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of IC50 variability in Figure 6B.

claim: Cancer cells that survived drug therapy rapidly reignited cell proliferation after drug release.
source: In general, cancer cells that survived drug therapy rapidly reignited cell proliferation after drug release.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of viable nuclei over time shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claim: Inhibition of the EGFR-RAS-ERK pathway predominantly inhibits cell-cycle progression in KRAS mutant CRC organoids.
source: In summary, these data indicate that inhibition of the EGFR-RAS-ERK pathway, independent of inhibitor combination, predominantly inhibits cell-cycle progression in KRAS mutant CRC organoids.
evidence: This is supported by the drug response and recovery data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Dual inhibition of the EGFR-MEK-ERK pathway induces a G1 cell cycle arrest in RAS mutant tumor cells.
source: Indicative of a G1 arrest, we observed a sharp decline in the amount of RAS mutant tumor cells in S-phase using inhibitor combinations EGFRi/MEKi and MEKi/ERKi, while a similar fraction of cells accumulated in G1 (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry cell cycle analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Almost no EdU incorporation was detected during drug treatment with dual inhibition of the EGFR-MEK-ERK signaling pathway.
source: In agreement with the previous cell cycle analysis, almost no EdU incorporation was detected in the presence of inhibitor combinations EGFRi/MEKi and MEKi/ERKi (no cells in S-phase) (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by EdU incorporation imaging shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The vast majority of growth-arrested tumor cells incorporated EdU during the first three days after drug withdrawal.
source: However, during the first three days after drug withdrawal, the vast majority of growth-arrested tumor cells incorporated EdU again, suggesting renewed proliferative activity in virtually all tumor cells, thereby excluding the presence of senescence or minor subpopulations being responsible for restored growth (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by EdU incorporation imaging after drug withdrawal shown in Figure 8C.

claim: A delay of about 20-24 hr was observed after withdrawal of EGFRi/MEKi drugs before observing numerous mitotic events again.
source: Indeed, in line with a G1 arrest, we observed a delay of about 20–24 hr after withdrawal of the drugs (EGFRi/MEKi) before observing numerous mitotic events again in all regions of the arrested organoids (Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1 and Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging and quantification of mitotic events shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Combined inhibition of anti-apoptotic BCL2 family members and effectors of the RAS pathway can effectively induce cell death in KRAS mutant cancers.
source: As opposed to this, it has been reported that combined inhibition of anti-apoptotic BCL2 family members and effectors of the RAS pathway can effectively induce cell death in KRAS mutant cancers (Corcoran et al., 2013; Hata et al., 2014, 2015; Tan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Corcoran et al., 2013; Hata et al., 2014, 2015; and Tan et al., 2013.

claim: Clinical application of BCL2/BCLXL inhibitors is hindered by on-target toxicity of BCLXL inhibition in blood platelets.
source: Unfortunately, clinical application of BCL2/BCLXL inhibitors is hindered by on-target toxicity of BCLXL inhibition in blood platelets (Hata et al., 2015) and might therefore strongly benefit from strategies that allow minimized doses.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hata et al., 2015.

claim: Navitoclax combined with afatinib, selumetinib, or both is more efficient in antagonizing tumor organoid growth than any of the related monotherapies.
source: Indeed, straightforward ATP-based screening confirmed that navitoclax, when combined with afatinib (Figure 9A, left panel), selumetinib (Figure 9A, middle panel), or both (Figure 9A, right panel) is far more efficient in antagonizing tumor organoid growth than any of the related monotherapies.
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Robust dual inhibition of the EGFR-RAS-ERK pathway is exceptionally potent in sensitizing navitoclax-induced effects.
source: Importantly, regarding the dose-limiting effects of navitoclax, we show that robust dual inhibition of the EGFR-RAS-ERK pathway (1 µM afatinib/1 µM selumetinib) is exceptionally potent in sensitizing navitoclax-induced effects (Figure 9A, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Low amounts of navitoclax (65 nM) only induce cell death in combination with effective inhibition of the RAS pathway using high concentrations of afatinib and selumetinib.
source: Low amounts of navitoclax (65 nM) only induce cell death in combination with effective inhibition of the RAS pathway using a high concentrations of afatinib and selumetinib.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The more efficient inhibition of the RAS pathway is achieved, the less navitoclax is required.
source: Exploring optimal drug concentrations reveal that the more effective inhibition of the RAS pathway is achieved (dual targeting and high concentrations), the less navitoclax is required.
evidence: This is supported by full matrix screen data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Venetoclax, a BCL2-specific inhibitor, is not able to reproduce the effects of navitoclax (BCL2/BCLXL).
source: Venotoclax, a BCL2-specific inhibitor, is not able to copy the effects of navitoclax (BCL2/BCLXL).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of venetoclax and navitoclax in full matrix screens shown in Figure 9D.

claim: It is BCLXL that protects against apoptosis upon targeted inhibition of a mutant RAS pathway in CRC organoids.
source: Furthermore, venetoclax, a BCL2-specific inhibitor, is unable to reproduce the effects of navitoclax (BCL2/BCLXLi) (Figure 9D), suggesting that in agreement with the reported findings in lung cancer (Corcoran et al., 2013), it is BCLXL that protects against apoptosis upon targeted inhibition of a mutant RAS pathway in CRC organoids (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of venetoclax vs navitoclax shown in Figure 9D and supported by citation to Corcoran et al., 2013.

claim: For KRAS mutant tumor organoid P26T, similar drug sensitivities were observed in vitro as in vivo upon xenotransplantation.
source: Importantly, for KRAS mutant tumor organoid P26T we observed similar drug sensitivities in vitro as in vivo upon xenotransplantation.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of in vitro (Figure 1) and in vivo (Figure 2) drug response data.

claim: The sensitivity of RAS WT colon cancer for EGFRi may represent the dependency of normal colon stem cells on EGFR signaling activity.
source: This may imply that the sensitivity of RAS WT colon cancer for EGFRi is not an acquired oncogene-addiction, but merely represents the dependency of normal colon (stem) cells on EGFR signaling activity (Wong et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the similar drug responses in normal and tumor organoids and supported by citation to Wong et al., 2012.

claim: One of the direct side effects of anti-EGFR monotherapy is diarrhea.
source: Indeed, one of the direct side effects of anti-EGFR monotherapy is diarrhea (Miroddi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Miroddi et al., 2015.

claim: Anti-EGFR therapy in patients with KRAS WT colon tumors is standard of care.
source: Anti-EGFR therapy in patients with KRAS WT colon tumors is standard of care, whereas patients with RAS mutant tumors are excluded.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge.

claim: Patients with RAS mutant tumors are excluded from anti-EGFR therapy.
source: Anti-EGFR therapy in patients with KRAS WT colon tumors is standard of care, whereas patients with RAS mutant tumors are excluded.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge.

claim: Drug treatments targeting the EGFR-RAS-ERK and the PI-3K/AKT cascades, including combinations thereof, are largely ineffective in RAS mutant CRC organoids.
source: Our analyses confirm that drug treatments targeting the EGFR-RAS-ERK and the PI-3K/AKT cascades, including combinations thereof, are largely ineffective in RAS mutant CRC organoids.
evidence: This is supported by drug screening data shown in Figures 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Combination treatment of EGFR-MEK-ERK pathway inhibitors may decrease the potency of low-abundant RAS mutant subclones to initiate tumor-relapse during therapy against a predominantly KRAS WT tumor.
source: Furthermore, combination treatments may decrease the potency of low-abundant RAS mutant subclones to initiate tumor-relapse during therapy against a predominantly KRAS WT tumor (Misale et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Misale et al., 2015.

claim: The combined inhibition of pan-HER and MEK is currently tested in patients with RAS mutant cancers in several clinical trials.
source: The combined inhibition of pan-HER and MEK is currently tested in patients with RAS mutant cancers in several clinical trials (e.g. NCT02450656, NCT02230553 and NCT02039336).
evidence: This is supported by references to clinical trial identifiers.

claim: The combined inhibition of MEK and ERK is currently in clinical trials.
source: An alternative combination that is currently in clinical trials is the combined inhibition of MEK and ERK (NCT02457793).
evidence: This is supported by reference to clinical trial identifier.

claim: Resistance to targeted inhibition of RAF and MEK often involves reactivation of ERK.
source: The rationale behind this combination is the notion that resistance to targeted inhibition of RAF and MEK often involves reactivation of ERK (Ryan et al., 2015), while suboptimal suppression of ERK activity in RAF mutant cancers may underlie the limited efficacy (Bollag et al., 2010; Corcoran et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ryan et al., 2015; Bollag et al., 2010; and Corcoran et al., 2015.

claim: Dual inhibition of MEK and ERK induced cell-cycle arrest rather than cell death in RAS mutant CRC organoids.
source: Although our RAS mutant CRC organoids showed sensitivity to dual inhibition of MEK and ERK, also this drug combination induced cell-cycle arrest rather than cell death, questioning whether it will be sufficient for the treatment of RAS mutant CRC.
evidence: This is supported by drug response data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Effective inhibition of the EGFR-MEK-ERK pathway through combinatorial targeting significantly primes cytostatic RAS mutant cancer cells for apoptosis.
source: With respect to clinical applications, we here report that effective inhibition of the EGFR-MEK-ERK pathway through combinatorial targeting does significantly prime the cytostatic RAS mutant cancer cells for apoptosis.
evidence: This is supported by the navitoclax sensitization data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Triple combination therapy with low concentrations of navitoclax (50 mg/kg; five days on, two days off) proved to be too toxic for the mice.
source: However, triple combination therapy with low concentrations of navitoclax (50 mg/kg; five days on, two days off) proved to be too toxic for the mice (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: Drug phenotypes observed in organoids appear representative for previously reported responses in vivo.
source: Importantly, the drug phenotypes that we observe in the organoids appear representative for previous reported responses in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with published PDX data and the xenograft experiments performed in this study.

claim: Organoid collections will facilitate the identification and optimization of effective targeted therapies.
source: We believe that organoid collections will facilitate the identification and optimization of effective targeted therapies, since drug screens can be performed at a scale that is currently unprecedented when using resource-intensive PDX models.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the demonstrated capabilities of organoid screening in this study.

claim: Novel drugs should be tested on a panel of tumor organoids before their use in clinical trials.
source: Due to the reliability and scalability of tumor organoids as a model system, we advocate that novel drugs should be tested on a panel of tumor organoids before their use in clinical trials.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the study.
